summaries.summary: The image explains 'Why mapping genes!!!' and highlights two main approaches: Family-based Linkage mapping and LD-based Association mapping. It describes Family-based Linkage mapping as QTL mapping, which involves constructing linkage maps and conducting QTL analysis to identify genomic regions associated with traits. The LD-based Association mapping is shown with a question mark, indicating it is the focus of the query. The source is Mackay & Powell 2007.
key_facts: Two main approaches to gene mapping: Family-based Linkage mapping and LD-based Association mapping.
Family-based Linkage mapping is also known as QTL mapping, genetic mapping, gene tagging, or family-based mapping.
LD-based Association mapping is presented as the second approach, with a question mark indicating it is the focus of the query.
The source of the information is Mackay & Powell 2007.
visible_text: Find molecular markers linked to target genes and then used in MAS

Constructing linkage maps and conducting QTL analysis–to identify genomic regions associated with traits–is known as QTL mapping (also genetic, ‘gene’ or ‘genome’ mapping/ gene tagging/ Family based mapping)

summaries.summary: This page explains Association Mapping, also called linkage disequilibrium mapping, as a method to determine marker-trait associations using Linkage Disequilibrium. It highlights that its power depends on the strength of correlation between the genotyped marker and the functional variant. The diagram illustrates two types of association: indirect and direct, linking a typed marker locus to a phenotype via a haplotype and an unobserved casual locus.
